beats.text: December fourth, eighteen seventy-two. A ship drifts across the Atlantic. Sails up. And nobody is on board.
Ten people. Gone. And to this day, nobody knows why.
Her name: the Mary Celeste. Captain Benjamin Briggs had taken his wife Sarah and their two-year-old daughter Sophia along.
The sailors who found her saw something strange. The ship could still sail. Six months of food. The crew's things, still there.
But the lifeboat was gone. One pump was taken apart. And there was water in the hold.
The last log entry: November twenty-fifth, near the island of Santa Maria. Then, nine days of silence.
In the hold: one thousand seven hundred and one barrels of alcohol. Nine of them were empty.
Some said: pirates. The newspapers printed it. Others blamed mutiny, a sea monster, even something from the sky.
A young Arthur Conan Doyle even wrote a made-up story about it. Many readers thought it was true.
So a court in Gibraltar looked for proof. No sign of a fight. No crime.
The most likely idea: Briggs feared the ship was sinking, or that the alcohol might explode. And he ordered everyone into the little boat.
But the lifeboat was never found. Neither was anyone in it.
A ship that could have saved them all, and ten people who left it. Nobody knows what really happened.

sources: Mary Celeste: found 4 Dec 1872 by the Dei Gratia (Capt. David Morehouse) between the Azores and Portugal; left New York 7 Nov 1872 for Genoa with 1,701 barrels of (denatured) alcohol; 10 aboard: Capt. Benjamin S. Briggs, wife Sarah, daughter Sophia (2), 7 crew; ship seaworthy, ~6 months of food and water, crew's belongings left; lifeboat missing; one pump disassembled, sounding rod on deck, ~3.5 ft of water in the hold; last log entry 25 Nov 1872, 8 a.m., near Santa Maria (Azores); 9 barrels empty when unloaded in Genoa. Gibraltar Vice-Admiralty Court salvage inquiry 1873: no evidence of foul play. Sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica; Smithsonian Magazine (2007, 'Abandoned Ship: The Mary Celeste'); Wikipedia 'Mary Celeste'.
Boston Post, 24 Feb 1873 (reprinted New York Times 26 Feb 1873): 'seized by pirates' – public domain clipping, Wikimedia Commons.
Arthur Conan Doyle, 'J. Habakuk Jephson's Statement', Cornhill Magazine, Jan 1884 (fiction, published anonymously; some readers took it as fact).

Most-cited explanation (abandonment in the yawl for fear of sinking/explosion) is a hypothesis; the fate of the 10 is unknown. Sea monster / 'something from the sky' = popular claims only, no evidence.
